---
title: 'Use secrets in a pipeline'
status: implemented
description: 'Store credentials as encrypted, write-only secrets and reference them from commands and env values.'
---

Store tokens, API keys and store credentials as secrets instead of pipeline
`env` values. Oore encrypts each value with the instance encryption key, never
returns it from the API, and masks it as `***` in build logs.

## What you need

- Project developer, maintainer, instance admin, or instance owner access for
  project and pipeline secrets.
- Instance admin or owner access for instance secrets.

## Scopes

A secret belongs to one scope. A build sees the secrets of its pipeline, its
project and the instance. When two scopes define the same name, the narrower
scope wins: pipeline over project, project over instance.

| Scope    | API base                              | Who can write              |
| -------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Instance | `/v1/secrets`                         | Instance admin or owner    |
| Project  | `/v1/projects/{project_id}/secrets`   | Project developer or above |
| Pipeline | `/v1/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/secrets` | Project developer or above |

Listing returns names and timestamps only. Anyone who can read the project can
see which names exist; nobody can read a value back, including the person who
wrote it.

## 1. Create a secret

Add the secret in the scope that matches who should use it:

- For every pipeline on the instance, open **Settings > Secrets**.
- For every pipeline in one project, open the project's **Settings** tab.
- For one pipeline, open the pipeline's **Secrets** tab.

Select **Add secret**, enter the **Name** and **Value**, and save. To change a
value later, use **Replace value**. The next build uses the new value. Builds
already running keep the old one.

Names follow environment variable rules (`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`, at most 128
characters). Values can be up to 64 KiB, which fits a Google Play service
account JSON file.

From the API, send the secret to the scope's base path:

```bash
curl -X POST "$OORE_URL/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/secrets" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN", "value": "sntrys_..."}'
```

To rotate, send `PUT .../secrets/{name}` with `{"value": "..."}`. To remove,
send `DELETE .../secrets/{name}`. Each change is written to the audit log.
Deleting a secret that a pipeline uses as its Google Play service account
returns `409 secret_in_use` and names those pipelines. Point them at another
secret first, or add `?force=true` to delete it anyway. A pipeline that would
fall back to a secret of the same name in a wider scope, such as an instance
`PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, does not block the delete.

## 2. Reference it

Use `${{ secrets.NAME }}` in an `env` value or in any command:

```yaml
env:
  - key: SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN
    value: ${{ secrets.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN }}
commands:
  post_build:
    - ./scripts/upload-symbols.sh --token "${{ secrets.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN }}"
```

- In an `env` value, the reference is replaced with the secret value before
  the step starts.
- In a command, the reference becomes the shell variable
  `${OORE_SECRET_NAME}`, which the runner sets for that build. Quote it as you
  would any shell variable. The value is never pasted into the command text.
- Env values that come from a secret are left out of the
  `--dart-define-from-file` file, so they are not compiled into the app. Pass
  one explicitly with `--dart-define` if the app really needs it.
- Only `${{ secrets.NAME }}` is supported inside `${{ }}`. Any other
  expression, or a reference to a secret that does not exist in any visible
  scope, fails the build before a step runs.

## Verify the result

Any line a step prints that contains a secret value shows `***` in its place.
For multi-line values such as JSON keys, each longer line of the value is
masked as well. Masking matches exact text, so a value that a step transforms
(for example, base64-encodes) is not recognised; avoid printing derived forms.

Run a build that uses the secret. The step that reads it succeeds, and the
log shows `***` wherever the value would appear.

## Troubleshooting

**The build fails before its first step with an unknown secret**

No visible scope defines that name. Check the spelling, and add the secret
to the pipeline, its project, or the instance.

**The value appears in the log**

The step printed a transformed form of the value, such as base64. Masking
matches exact text only. Stop printing the value, then rotate it.
